title: Hit rates, skew and eviction
summary: The miss rate is what the database feels. Working sets and Zipf skew, sizing a cache for the hot set, LRU, LFU and W-TinyLFU, Redis maxmemory policies, and the redis-cli commands that show what your cache is doing.

steps.title: The database feels the misses
body: A cache in front of a database turns `reads` into `reads × (1 − hit ratio)` database reads. The hit ratio
looks like a vanity number, but the **miss ratio** is the one that decides the database size:
| Hit ratio | Miss ratio | DB reads at 20,000 reads/s |
Going from 90 % to 99 % sounds like a 10 % improvement. For the database it is a **10× drop** in load.
The flip side: a cache that drops from 99 % to 90 % (a deploy that changed key names, a restart) sends
10× the reads to a database that was sized for the cache being there. Seniors size the database for
the realistic **worst** hit ratio, or protect it (next lesson).

steps.explain: The database load falls with the miss ratio: every percentage point near the top of the hit ratio is worth more than the one before.

steps.title: Skew: a small hot set takes most reads
body: Real traffic is not uniform. A few products, profiles or videos take most of the reads. A common model is
**Zipf**: the key of rank *i* gets traffic in proportion to `1 / i^s`, with `s` near 1 for many web
workloads. With one million keys and `s = 1`:
| Hottest keys cached | Share of keys | Share of reads they serve |
- **Working set**: the keys read within a time window (say, an hour). Size the cache for the hot part
of the working set, not for the whole table.
Two consequences. First, a cache much smaller than the data can still have a high hit ratio. Second, the
last few percent are expensive: each extra point of hit ratio needs many more cold keys in memory. Measure
the curve (hit ratio against cache size) on real traffic before buying memory.

prompt: A catalogue has 50 million products of about 2 KB each (100 GB). Logs show the top 2 million products take
about 90 % of reads, and the database can comfortably serve 15 % of today's reads. What is a sensible first
cache size?
options: About 4-6 GB of values plus overhead, holding the hot 2 million products
100 GB, so every product is cached
200 MB, because caches should be small
No cache: add read replicas instead
steps.explain: 2 million × 2 KB = 4 GB of values; Redis adds per-key overhead (tens of bytes plus the key), so budget roughly 5-6 GB and leave memory headroom. A 90 % hit ratio leaves 10 % of reads for the database, under its 15 % budget. Caching all 100 GB costs 20× the memory for the last 10 % of reads.

steps.title: Eviction: who leaves when memory is full
body: - **LRU** (least recently used): evict the key untouched for longest. Simple and good for recency, but a
one-off scan (a batch job reading every product once) pushes the whole hot set out.
- **LFU** (least frequently used): evict the key with the lowest access count, so a scan does little
harm. Needs counters that **decay**, or yesterday's hits keep stale keys forever.
- **W-TinyLFU** (Caffeine on the JVM): a small LRU window for new keys plus a frequency sketch that
decides whether a newcomer may replace a victim. Near-optimal hit ratios on most traces.
Redis and Valkey choose with `maxmemory-policy`. Their LRU and LFU are **approximate**: they sample a few
keys (`maxmemory-samples`, default 5) and evict the best candidate among them.
| Policy | Evicts |
| `noeviction` (the default) | nothing: writes fail with an OOM error when memory is full |
| `allkeys-lru` / `allkeys-lfu` | any key, by recency / frequency |
| `volatile-lru` / `volatile-lfu` | only keys that have a TTL |
| `volatile-ttl` | keys with a TTL, soonest to expire first |
| `allkeys-random` / `volatile-random` | a random key |
For a pure cache, `allkeys-lfu` or `allkeys-lru` is the usual choice. `noeviction` is right when Redis
holds data you cannot lose (queues, locks), and then you must alert on memory.

steps.prompt: Match each situation to the policy or behaviour it calls for.
pairs: A pure cache whose hot set is stable for days
A nightly job reads every key once and wrecks the hit ratio
Use LFU (or W-TinyLFU) so a scan cannot flush the hot set
The same Redis holds session data without TTLs and cache keys with TTLs
`volatile-lru`: only keys with a TTL may be evicted
Redis holds a job queue that must never drop entries
Writes start failing with `OOM command not allowed`

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: looking inside a cache
steps.body: When the cache is slow, cold or full, these show you why. All of them work on Redis and on Valkey.

toolkit.what: Server counters since start-up: hits, misses, evictions, expirations. Hit ratio = hits / (hits + misses); compare two snapshots a minute apart for the current rate.
flags: reads that found / did not find the key
keys removed because memory was full
toolkit.when: first look at a cache that seems cold

toolkit.what: Scans the keyspace and lists the most frequently used keys. Only works with an LFU `maxmemory-policy`, because it reads the LFU counters.
flags: report hot keys from LFU counters
sleep 0.1 s between SCAN batches to go easy on production
toolkit.when: one cache node is far busier than the others

toolkit.what: Scans for the largest keys by element count (`--bigkeys`) or by memory (`--memkeys`). Big keys make single commands slow and block the server.
toolkit.when: latency spikes that line up with one command

toolkit.what: Bytes a key and its value take, including overhead. Multiply by the key count to size a cache.
flags: examine every element of a collection (slow on huge keys)

toolkit.what: The LFU access counter of one key (LFU policies only). A quick check of whether a suspected hot key really is hot.
Changes the eviction policy at run time. Persist it in the config file too, or it is lost on restart.
flags: the memory limit eviction starts at
write the running config back to the file
toolkit.when: a pure cache running with the `noeviction` default

toolkit.what: Pings the server continuously and prints min, max and average round trip in ms. Separates "Redis is slow" from "my client or network is slow".
flags: a new line every 15 s instead of one running total

steps.prompt: Switch a cache to frequency-based eviction, then list its hottest keys gently.
steps.explain: `--hotkeys` reads the LFU counters, so it refuses to run unless the policy is one of the `*-lfu` ones.

prompt: **Symptom first.** Database reads doubled overnight with no traffic change. Two snapshots of the cache, 60 s
apart:
options: The cache is full and evicting about 1,700 keys a second; the hit ratio in this minute is only 58 %. The hot set has outgrown 12 GB: add memory (or shards), and check for new big keys
The hit ratio is 90 %, which is healthy; look at the database instead
explain: Use the deltas, not the totals: 147,000 hits and 105,000 misses in the minute is 58 %. The totals (90 %)
hide the change because they include weeks of history. Memory at the limit plus a fast-growing
`evicted_keys` means keys are pushed out before they are read again.

steps.title: Hit ratio and database load
prompt: Write three functions:
- `double HitRatio(long hits, long misses)`: hits divided by all lookups; `0` when there were none.
- `int DbReadsPerSecond(int readsPerSecond, double hitRatio)`: the reads that miss, **rounded** to the
nearest whole number.
- `double RequiredHitRatio(int readsPerSecond, int dbCapacity)`: the lowest hit ratio that keeps database
reads at or under `dbCapacity`; `0` when the database can take every read on its own.
`DbReadsPerSecond(20000, 0.99)` is `200`. `RequiredHitRatio(20000, 1500)` is `0.925`.
solution: double HitRatio(long hits, long misses) => hits + misses == 0 ? 0 : (double)hits / (hits + misses);
int DbReadsPerSecond(int readsPerSecond, double hitRatio) => (int)Math.Round(readsPerSecond * (1 - hitRatio));
hints: Cast to `double` before dividing, or integer division gives 0.
Required hit ratio: the database may take at most `dbCapacity / reads` of the reads; the cache must take the rest.
template: Dojo.Eq("hit ratio from the 09:00-09:01 deltas", 0.583, Math.Round(HitRatio(147000, 105000), 3));
Dojo.Eq("required hit ratio for a 1,500/s database", 0.925, Math.Round(RequiredHitRatio(20000, 1500), 3));
Dojo.Eq("a database that copes alone needs no cache", 0.0, RequiredHitRatio(1000, 1500));

steps.title: An O(1) LRU cache
prompt: Write a generic class `LruCache<TKey, TValue> where TKey : notnull` that holds at most `capacity` entries
and evicts the **least recently used** one, with every operation in O(1):
- `LruCache(int capacity)`: throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` when `capacity <= 0`.
- `bool TryGet(TKey key, out TValue value)`: a hit marks the key as most recently used.
- `void Put(TKey key, TValue value)`: inserts or updates (an update also marks it most recently used and
never evicts). Inserting into a full cache first evicts the least recently used key.
- `int Count` and `int Evictions`.
Use a `Dictionary` from key to a `LinkedListNode`, and a `LinkedList` kept in recency order (most recent
first), so you never search the list.
starter: class LruCache<TKey, TValue> where TKey : notnull
public bool TryGet(TKey key, out TValue value) { value = default!; return false; }
public void Put(TKey key, TValue value) { }
solution: class LruCache<TKey, TValue> where TKey : notnull
readonly Dictionary<TKey, LinkedListNode<(TKey Key, TValue Value)>> map = new();
readonly LinkedList<(TKey Key, TValue Value)> order = new();
public int Evictions { get; private set; }
public bool TryGet(TKey key, out TValue value)
public void Put(TKey key, TValue value)
hints: Store `(key, value)` in each list node, so evicting `order.Last` tells you which dictionary entry to remove.
Moving a node to the front is `order.Remove(node); order.AddFirst(node);`, both O(1) when you hold the node.

require.message: Keeps recency order in a LinkedList

template: Dojo.Check("a is a hit", dojoL.TryGet("a", out var dojoA) && dojoA == 1, "TryGet(\"a\") should return 1");
Dojo.Check("b was evicted: a was used more recently", !dojoL.TryGet("b", out _), "b should be gone");
Dojo.Check("a survived because it was read", dojoL.TryGet("a", out _), "a should still be cached");
Dojo.Check("c is cached", dojoL.TryGet("c", out var dojoC) && dojoC == 3, "TryGet(\"c\") should return 3");
Dojo.Eq("count never exceeds the capacity", 2, dojoL.Count);
Dojo.Eq("updating a key does not evict", 1, dojoL.Evictions);
Dojo.Check("the update made a most recent, so c goes", !dojoL.TryGet("c", out _), "c should be evicted");
Dojo.Check("a has the updated value", dojoL.TryGet("a", out var dojoA2) && dojoA2 == 10, "a should be 10");
for (var dojoI = 0; dojoI < 200000; dojoI++) dojoBig.Put(dojoI, dojoI);
Dojo.Eq("200,000 inserts keep exactly 1,000 keys", 1000, dojoBig.Count);
Dojo.Check("the newest key is cached", dojoBig.TryGet(199999, out _), "199999 should be cached");
Dojo.Check("an old key is gone", !dojoBig.TryGet(5, out _), "5 should be evicted");
steps.explain: This is the structure behind most in-process caches and a staple interview question. Redis does not keep a global list (too much memory per key); it samples keys and evicts the oldest of the sample, which is close enough at a fraction of the cost.
